Creating the largest neutrino detectors in the world

Can someone explain why they build neutrino detectors underground? They could travel though a million miles of lead and have a good chance of coming out the other side. A little bit of dirt seems unnecessary.

Our neighborhood of the universe has a lot of cosmic rays zipping through outer space -- particles like protons that have immense kinetic energy. When a cosmic rays hits the atmosphere, it collides with an atom and spews out a shower of other particles. The shower includes a lot of muons, which are able to penetrate enormous distances through solid rock, easily hundreds of meters. (Muons are heavy enough to kick electrons out of the way with impunity, but light enough that they bounce off protons. So they have an uncanny ability to go through everyday matter.)

There are rather a lot of these cosmic muons. If I remember right, about one muon per square centimeter per minute at ground level. A quick estimate says that this experiment would "see" about 500,000 muons per second if it were built at ground level. That would cause serious interference with the neutrinos they hope to detect, which are probably number only a few thousand per year.

So they build most neutrino detectors deep underground. The rock absorbs most of the cosmic ray muons. If you're looking for a dim flash, it is easier to spot it in a dark room than staring into the sun.
